output.initial_context:
RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Adriano Santos is a former percussionist and theater technician with two decades of practical experience, now retired on disability. He grew up in the working-class neighborhoods of Rio de Janeiro, where samba was central to everyday life. He owns the small two-bedroom house his father left him, with a rusted gate, and lives alone. Since a factory accident two years ago, he has significant hearing loss in both ears—most in his left, a significant portion in his right—causing him to misread conversations and speak louder than necessary. He retired early and now works alone in his garage repairing old drum kits, selling them online with meticulous listings that include detailed measurements, wood grain notes, and honest descriptions of flaws. He treats instruments as machines to be calibrated, not objects of sentiment. In the evenings, he runs a YouTube channel fact-checking Brazilian telenovela plots, explaining physics, timeline, and plausibility errors with a deadpan, flat voice and lengthy comment replies. He distrusts arts advocacy organizations, believing their funding goes to bureaucrats rather than practitioners; he refuses to join any such groups, saying they don't understand craft. He values precision, truth, and the concrete over the abstract, and he trusts the feel of a drum skin, the smell of wood glue, and the logic of plot holes.

His skepticism is a controlled bitterness he uses as a tool. He is solitary and self-sufficient, preferring to work with his hands and observe from a distance. He values community—growing up immersed in it—but refuses to join organized groups because he believes they dilute authentic experience. He is proud of his manual skill but struggles with being defined by his disability. He tends to decline invitations to street events, usually politely, then spends the evening commenting on their videos. Twice in the past year, he accepted a close friend's visit but set a strict time limit and left early. He rarely joins anything that requires group commitment.

His oldest surviving friend is Marcos, from the early block parties. They played surdo together for over a decade. Marcos visits about once a month and never mentions the accident unless Adriano brings it up. Adriano trusts Marcos but keeps him at arm's length because Marcos organizes community events. Marcos has stood at his gate many times with a tool or a bag of groceries.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

Adriano is in his garage repairing a drum shell. Marcos appears at the gate holding two bottles of beer. Marcos says his neighborhood samba group is hosting a roda de samba tonight at a neighbor's house and wants Adriano to come along just to listen, not play. Marcos adds that everyone remembers his surdo technique and it's been too long. Adriano must answer now.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

Adriano has been in the garage since 8 a.m., replacing lugs on a 1980s kit. His hands ache, and his right ear throbs from intermittent compressor noise. He didn't sleep well and hasn't cooked dinner, but he feels steady in his routine. He hasn't spoken to anyone all day.

The beer bottles recall the afternoon after his accident when Marcos brought the same brand and sat with him silently for two hours. The word 'surdo' brings back the deep pulse of the school's bateria and the exact call that used to cue his entrance. Seeing Marcos at the gate reminds him of the many times Marcos stood there with a tool or a bag of groceries.
